query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high‐entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a coherent, protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C is primarily governed by the nature of the reactive element X: additions of Al or Si promote the formation of slow‐growing, adherent oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) via controlled metal and oxygen diffusion at the surface, whereas Mn forms faster-growing, volatile manganese oxides that cannot accommodate internal growth stresses and therefore crack and spall. The resulting behavior in Al- or Si-alloyed materials is expected to be superior (i.e. more stable and protective oxide scale) compared to Mn-alloyed or baseline CrFeCoNi alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys synthesized to produce a homogenized single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with controlled elemental compositions (with minor alloy additions of Al, Si, or Mn, typically within the same concentration range).
generation.intervention: Engineer the alloy compositions by adding a fixed amount of Al, Si, or Mn (keeping other elements constant) and then subject each variant to high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.conditions: Expose the samples to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at a temperature above 900 °C (for instance, at ~950 °C) for an extended period (e.g. 100 hours) under a well-defined oxygen partial pressure (e.g. 1 atm air) to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and morphology of the oxide scale—specifically whether a continuous, adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 or SiO2 layer forms versus a discontinuous, volatile, and stress-prone manganese oxide layer—is the structural feature that mediates the observed performance.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism involves differential oxidation kinetics and metal diffusion behavior: Al and Si, having strong oxygen affinities, form compact, low-growth-rate oxide scales that relieve internal stresses and reduce further oxygen ingress. In contrast, Mn oxidizes more rapidly to form less stable oxides that develop high internal stresses, frequently leading to cracking or spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing Al or Si will develop and maintain a coherent, stable, and protective oxide scale with lower spallation and mass loss compared to Mn-containing alloys or baseline CrFeCoNi alloys, which will exhibit unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide layers under the identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of a CrFeCoNi alloy without additional reactive elements (or with Mn as a contrasting additive) serves as the baseline, where the absence of Al or Si should result in a less stable oxide coverage.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloys processed to form single- or multiphase solid solutions with low to moderate X-element contents (e.g., up to ~10 at.%). It is valid under oxidation test conditions above 900 °C in atmospheres with oxygen partial pressures similar to 1 atm air. Extrapolation beyond these processing or exposure boundaries may not be justified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative thresholds for alloying additions, diffusion kinetics, and the relative stresses generated during oxide growth still carry uncertainty. The influence of multiphase microstructures might also modify oxidation behavior, necessitating further refinement of the mechanistic details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with equivalent processing routes, where X is systematically varied among Al, Si, Mn, and a control sample without X. Expose all samples to an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air at 1 atm) at approximately 950 °C for 100 hours. Evaluate the nature of the oxide scales using microscopy (SEM), phase analysis (XRD), and quantify oxide spallation through mass loss measurements.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (SEM/optical microscopy)
Mass change or mass loss due to spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al- and Si-containing alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., lower mass loss and maintenance of coherent oxide film) compared to Mn-containing or baseline alloys under the same conditions, or if Mn-containing alloys unexpectedly form similarly protective oxide scales, the hypothesis is falsified.
